evidence_add.extracted: Table 4 prints, for drugs that included illicit benzodiazepines, a common cumulative odds ratio of 19.918 (95% CI 8.573 to 46.273). Its category probabilities after a positive result are 0.032, 0.701 and 0.266 for less or none, same and more; after a negative result they are 0.009, 0.334 and 0.657 (the last with 95% CI 0.091 to 0.973). Editors' calculations: odds(0.032)/odds(0.009) = 3.640 and odds(1-0.266)/odds(1-0.657) = 5.285. Allowing each probability to vary by 0.0005 gives conservative ranges of 3.391-3.918 and 5.260-5.311: they are mutually disjoint and exclude the printed common odds ratio. Methods p. 3 describes applying a logistic function to a least-square mean to obtain the two cumulative probabilities over a balanced population. Under that procedure, if the probabilities and contrast use the same proportional-odds model and covariate weights, both cumulative-odds ratios would equal the common model contrast. Averaging probabilities first is a different procedure and can give other ratios; the mismatch does not establish that the fitted coefficient is wrong. Neither a replacement common odds ratio nor a corrected subgroup ordering is identified. No fitted model or prediction code is provided in the supplied paper. The printed overall common odds ratio is 4.373 (95% CI 3.448 to 5.545), with positive-result probabilities 0.090, 0.847 and 0.063, and negative-result probabilities 0.023, 0.752 and 0.225. Note [1] announces a number of participants per model that no column gives. Note [2] lists overdose in the past 30 days among the covariates; it was asked in the baseline survey (p. 2), and no overdose or other harm outcome is analysed. Only the any-change association was the primary hypothesis: the authors made no adjustment for multiple comparisons and call all other p-values descriptive (pp. 3, 5). In Table 3, after a positive against a negative result: took turns 0.24 against 0.19, used near someone who had naloxone 0.23 against 0.15, used less 0.11 against 0.02.
